statement: The system shall keep the X-38 flight-critical computer dependable even when parts of the system fail.
The system shall allow mission applications to continue performing their functions when parts of the system fail.
The system shall provide mission applications with reliable scheduling.
The system shall provide mission applications with reliable communication.
The system shall provide mission applications with reliable time services.
The system shall provide mission applications with reliable memory services.
The system shall provide mission applications with general system support.
The system shall hide the details of the underlying processor and operating system from mission applications.
The system shall detect faults.
The system shall coordinate redundant resources so that it can keep functioning through component failures.
The system shall support mission application developers and the flight software team as primary users.
The system shall behave predictably for mission application developers and the flight software team.
The system shall shield mission application developers and the flight software team from hardware and operating system details.
The system shall support redundancy management for systems and fault-tolerance engineers.
The system shall support fault detection for systems and fault-tolerance engineers.
The system shall ensure that the right component takes over when a failure occurs.
The system shall support certification concerns for NASA mission operations and safety/reliability stakeholders.
The system shall support recovery behavior for NASA mission operations and safety/reliability stakeholders.
The system shall keep the vehicle safe under failure conditions.
The services shall keep the vehicle running on the healthiest available redundant resource with as little interruption as possible.
The system shall bring a standby or peer instance into control after a component failure.
The system shall keep replicas synchronized closely enough that the transition is predictable and safe.
The system shall be designed to handle faults expected in a flight-critical redundant computer.
The system shall be designed to handle processor or service failures.
The system shall be designed to handle transient glitches.
The system shall be designed to handle timing problems.
The system shall be designed to handle software faults that can corrupt execution or communication.
The system shall not assume arbitrary Byzantine behavior unless it is explicitly designed and verified for that behavior.
Anything beyond the fault model that the redundancy and isolation scheme can actually tolerate shall be treated as out of scope.
The X-38 Fault Tolerant System Services should treat fully arbitrary Byzantine faults as out of scope.
The X-38 Fault Tolerant System Services should treat simultaneous loss of all redundant channels as out of scope.
The X-38 Fault Tolerant System Services should treat failures caused by hazards outside the computing system itself as out of scope.
The X-38 Fault Tolerant System Services should treat fault combinations that exceed the designed redundancy level as out of scope.
The out-of-scope fault conditions are excluded because the service layer cannot reliably recover from them.
The out-of-scope fault conditions are excluded to keep the service verifiable and certifiable within the hardware and redundancy architecture that X-38 actually has.
The verification approach shall include requirements-based verification.
The verification approach shall include design and fault-tree analysis.
The verification approach shall include simulation.
The verification approach shall include fault-injection testing.
The verification approach shall include integration testing on representative flight hardware or an equivalent rig.
The software shall demonstrate operation in normal cases.
The software shall recover within the timing and safety bounds required by the vehicle.
Approval evidence shall include traceability from requirements to tests.
Approval evidence shall include test results with pass/fail evidence.
In degraded or recovery modes, fault-tolerance functions shall take priority enough to protect the vehicle.
In degraded or recovery modes, nonessential mission work may be delayed or throttled.
When resources are tight or a failover is underway, safety-critical system services and the applications needed for control shall outrank lower-priority work.
The system shall provide fault tolerant services for the X-38 flight-critical computer.
The system shall support scheduling functions.
The system shall support communication functions.
The system shall support time functions.
The system shall support memory functions.
The system shall support system support functions.
The system shall perform fault detection.
The system shall perform fault isolation.
The system shall coordinate redundant resources.
The system shall support the needs of the X-38 flight software and mission operations side.
The system shall provide the required services through a redundant flight computer setup rather than relying on a single processor or operating system instance.
The system shall be more transparent to mission applications.
The system shall provide core capabilities needed by the user.
Health monitoring should be included as a supporting requirement for the system's main fault-tolerance goals.
Graceful degradation should be included as a supporting requirement for the system's main fault-tolerance goals.
The system shall prioritize fault detection and isolation with coordination of redundant resources as the highest priority feature.
The system shall recognize when a processor, task, or communication path is behaving abnormally.
The system shall watch for the main abnormal conditions first.
If automatic switching fails, the system shall keep the vehicle in the safest possible degraded mode and continue trying any available recovery actions.
The system shall alert the mission software or flight crew support functions so that the failure is visible.
The computing system shall keep the vehicle flying safely and predictably even if parts of the flight computer fail.
The computing system shall support mission applications with dependable timing.
The computing system shall support mission applications with dependable communication.
The computing system shall support mission applications with dependable system services.
The computing system shall detect faults quickly.
The computing system shall isolate faults so that redundant computer resources can take over or keep operating.
The operational situations that most shape the computing system's goals are component failures.
The computing system shall continue critical functions during a fault and still guide the vehicle to a safe outcome rather than losing control because one computing element failed.
The system shall support the crew return mission for the X-38 vehicle.
The service shall be maintained very conservatively.
Updates to the service shall go through a formal verification and test process.
Changes to mission logic shall preserve the same fault-tolerance behavior.
The service shall adapt if the vehicle or mission profile changes.
The mission applications shall be able to rely on the provided services as if they were stable infrastructure rather than something they must constantly defend against.
The system shall provide predictable behavior.
The service layer shall provide enough confidence for mission applications to make flight decisions and control actions without worrying about hidden processor or operating-system details.
Any change that affects how faults are detected, isolated, or recovered from shall justify a new verification cycle.
Changes to the underlying processor shall require re-verification if they could affect behavior under failure.
Any change that weakens isolation shall be treated as out of bounds unless it undergoes a full safety review.
The main day-to-day users are the mission applications and the flight software team.
Approval and oversight are handled by the systems and safety staff.
Mission operations and program management are involved at a higher level.
The runtime shall serve core flight-critical functions that keep the vehicle stable and bring it home safely.
The runtime shall support command functions that need dependable timing and coordination.
The runtime shall also be used by other onboard applications with direct flight-safety impact.
Approval shall require complete test results.
Approval shall require traceability to requirements.
Approval shall require clear sign-off that the change was analyzed for impact before flight use.
The vehicle should keep doing the right job even if a computer, task, or communication path misbehaves.
The runtime should switch to a safe alternate mode or a degraded mode.
The runtime should preserve control of mission-critical functions when switching to a safe alternate or degraded mode.
A redundant computer shall be a backup or parallel flight-critical processor arrangement that can take over if the primary side fails.
A redundant resource shall be any duplicate capability the runtime can use to keep going.
A redundant resource may include an alternate compute path.
A redundant resource may include a communication path.
A redundant resource may include a timing source.
A redundant resource may include stored state needed to preserve function after a fault.
The runtime shall rely on a second option rather than a single point of failure.
Mission time and scheduling services shall be available only while the runtime is in operational flight mode and the relevant computer is participating in the active control set.
If a request for mission time or scheduling services arrives outside the allowed window, the service shall reject it cleanly.
If a request for mission time or scheduling services arrives outside the allowed window, the service shall log it.
If a request for mission time or scheduling services arrives outside the allowed window, the service shall avoid disturbing any currently valid flight function.
System-support calls shall allow only operations that are safe in the current mode.
System-support calls shall fail closed if a request does not fit the current mode boundary.
The system shall bound and control the workload rather than allow open-ended execution.
The system shall ensure critical functions receive CPU time and meet their deadlines.
High-priority flight-control or fault-handling work shall be able to preempt lower-priority application activity.
Less critical tasks may have to defer or share resources when the system is under load.
The runtime shall arbitrate contention for important resources in a deterministic way.
The runtime shall make it possible to predict which application wins a contention and why.
Priority shall be the first rule for allocating the resource.
The most time-critical and safety-critical request shall receive the resource first.
If two requests have the same priority, the system shall use a deterministic tie-breaker.
The tie-breaker outcome shall be repeatable and reviewable.
The resource allocation rule may vary by resource type.
Timing or control resources shall be harder to delay than nonessential data services.
An urgent fault-recovery action shall override normal application use.
The system shall preempt a lower-urgency request when delaying the higher-urgency request would put safety or mission control at risk.
The system shall allow a higher-urgency request to wait only if the current holder can safely finish without affecting safety or mission control.
If the resource is free, the system shall grant the higher-urgency request immediately.
If the resource is already committed to a safety-critical action, the runtime shall protect that action and queue the lower-urgency request.
The system shall favor decisions that keep the vehicle safe and deterministic rather than decisions based only on arrival order.
A very limited housekeeping or recovery exception may be allowed for mission time or scheduling services.
Any housekeeping or recovery exception for mission time or scheduling services shall be tightly controlled and explicitly authorized.
The service layer shall handle flight-critical application data for guidance.
The service layer shall handle flight-critical application data for navigation.
The service layer shall handle flight-critical application data for control.
The service layer shall handle flight-critical application data for fault management.
The service layer shall handle flight-critical application data for timing.
The service layer shall handle command/status exchange between redundant computing elements.
The system shall preserve the data that mission applications need to make decisions and coordinate actions.
The data shall be tightly tied to real-time flight operations.
The data shall not be general-purpose user information.
Mission-to-subsystem message delivery shall be dependable.
Mission-to-subsystem message delivery shall not create duplicate actions in the receiver.
Mission-to-subsystem message delivery shall provide exactly-once behavior where it matters.
Mission-to-subsystem message delivery shall include a mechanism that makes duplicates harmless when exact-once delivery is not provided.
The sender shall know when a mission-to-subsystem message could not be delivered.
Ordering shall be preserved for related mission-to-subsystem messages.
Ordering shall be preserved especially across redundant computers or after recovery.
The system shall prevent out-of-order updates from causing the wrong flight state.
The system shall trigger a shift into safe return mode when failures threaten continued controlled flight.
The system shall trigger a shift into safe return mode when there is a loss of a critical computer lane.
The system shall trigger a shift into safe return mode when there are repeated faults in the active control path.
The system shall trigger a shift into safe return mode when a fault pattern indicates the system can no longer trust its current configuration.
The transition into safe return mode shall be immediate.
The transition into safe return mode shall be deterministic.
The transition into safe return mode shall be conservative.
The system shall move the vehicle to the most stable recoverable state available during the transition to safe return mode.
The system shall preserve fault evidence during the changeover to safe return mode.
The system shall keep any remaining redundant resources aligned during the changeover to safe return mode.
The fault-tolerant services requirements shall be anchored to the vehicle's return and crew safety function.

The system shall delay or suppress the shift into safe return mode only if there is strong evidence that the failure is being isolated and the vehicle can remain safely controlled long enough to avoid a worse transition.
Any delay in shifting into safe return mode shall be very short and bounded.
Any delay in shifting into safe return mode shall include strict monitoring.
If continued safe control cannot be confidently maintained, the system shall enter safe return mode immediately.
The fault detection and isolation logic shall treat repeated fault reports from the same lane as a strong sign that the fault is no longer contained.
The fault detection and isolation logic shall treat loss of agreement between redundant computers as a strong sign that the fault is no longer contained.
The fault detection and isolation logic shall treat missing or stale time updates as a strong sign that the fault is no longer contained.
The fault detection and isolation logic shall treat unresponsive critical services as a strong sign that the fault is no longer contained.

The fault detection and isolation logic shall treat evidence that a control channel or scheduled task is no longer executing within its expected timing window as a strong sign that the fault is no longer contained.
The fault detection and isolation logic shall enter safe return mode immediately if those conditions persist after a short verification cycle.

The system shall choose the safest state that preserves controlled flight and requires the fewest uncertain assumptions about the failed component when more than one stable recoverable state is possible.
If there is a tie, the system shall prefer the state that keeps the greatest amount of validated redundancy available and gives the flight crew or ground systems the clearest path to recovery.
The system shall retain the fault history that led to the transition.
The system shall retain fault codes.
Developers shall be able to use the mission services with minimal platform-specific setup.
The mission services shall expose a small, consistent interface.
The wiring and configuration shall be straightforward enough that a developer can focus on mission application logic.
The wiring and configuration shall not require developers to focus on fault-tolerant coordination mechanics.
Any specialized knowledge required to use the mission services shall be limited to clearly documented service contracts.
The system shall allow retries for mission-to-subsystem messages when the message is not safety-critical and a late duplicate would not cause a harmful action.
The system shall preserve message order for control updates and avoid dropping important messages.
The system shall tag each mission update with a unique sequence identifier or transaction identifier.
The receiver shall use the sequence identifier or transaction identifier to recognize duplicate mission updates and ignore them.
If delivery failure makes ordering uncertain, the system shall re-establish the stream and resend only after the receiver confirms where it left off.
The system shall prevent mission applications from handling redundancy management themselves.
The system shall sit underneath the mission software as a dependable platform service.
The system shall handle scheduling in the background.
The system shall handle communication in the background.
The system shall handle timing in the background.
The system shall handle memory support in the background.
The system shall handle fault isolation in the background.
The system shall be transparent most of the time in the mission workflow.
The system shall surface faults only when applications need to know about them.
The system shall surface state changes only when applications or operators need to know about them.
The system shall surface recovery needs only when applications or operators need to know about them.
The system shall support a phased transition for introducing the fault-tolerant service.
The system shall not replace the existing computing services in a big-bang migration.
The system shall allow the fault-tolerant service to run alongside the existing services during migration.
The system shall validate each part of the fault-tolerant service before it is relied upon in flight.
The system shall preserve current mission interfaces as much as possible when swapping the implementation underneath.
The system shall keep application changes small during the migration.
Any direct replacement of a service shall occur only after the new path has been proven equivalent or better under fault conditions.
The system shall perform state and configuration translation so the new service can take over without confusing the mission software.
The system shall preserve active task state where possible during the transition.
The system shall preserve timing references during the transition.
The system shall preserve communication endpoints during the transition.
The system shall preserve redundancy or health status that affects recovery decisions during the transition.
The system shall preserve fault history during any conversion for switchover.
The system shall preserve configuration values that determine how the system behaves after a switchover.
Applications shall use a single authoritative mission time service provided by the fault-tolerant layer instead of local processor clocks.
The mission time source shall stay consistent across redundant computers so applications can coordinate events and logs even after a lane fails over.
If there is a discrepancy, the service shall mask it from applications as much as possible and keep them on the same mission timeline.

The system shall not define a single fixed millisecond response-time value for all flight services because the required response time depends on the particular service and the control loop it supports.
Each flight service shall have a bounded, deterministic response time.
The system shall allow brief, predefined recovery windows during which a missed timing event does not immediately force safe return mode.
The system shall allow lower-priority tasks a greater timing tolerance than other tasks.
The system shall not allow flight-critical control channels the extra timing tolerance given to lower-priority tasks.
The system shall trigger fault isolation and a more protective response immediately when critical tasks experience repeated timing misses or when timing slip could affect vehicle safety.
The fault-tolerant platform service shall keep multiple paths active when redundancy management needs cross-checking.
The fault-tolerant platform service shall keep multiple paths active when it is still within a tolerated degrade mode.
When multiple paths are active, the applications shall continue to see one consistent service interface.
The system shall enforce strict partitioning so that one mission application cannot overwrite or starve another mission application.
The system shall ensure that a fault in one partition does not spread to the rest of the system.
The flight-critical services shall use mostly static or pre-allocated memory.
The flight-critical services shall avoid heavy dynamic allocation.
The redundant computer shall have protected regions for system support and health-management data.
The protected regions on the redundant computer shall keep system support and health-management data intact during failover or partial failures.
Protected regions on the redundant computer shall include redundancy-management state.
Protected regions on the redundant computer shall include fault logs.
Protected regions on the redundant computer shall include mission time state.
Protected regions on the redundant computer shall include scheduling metadata.
Protected regions on the redundant computer shall include recovery information needed to resume safely after a switchover.
Protected regions on the redundant computer shall include the minimal system-support functions needed to maintain communication and coordinate the surviving lane.
Access to protected regions shall be restricted whenever a component is suspected of being faulty.
Access to protected regions shall be preserved through failover or partial failure so the surviving side can keep operating without reinitializing critical state.
Mission applications shall only see the data they are authorized to use.
Mission applications shall not be able to write outside their own partition or service contract.
During fault detection or switchover, updates to shared mission state shall be controlled to prevent two conflicting writers.
The fault-tolerant layer shall arbitrate updates and allow only one trusted path to commit changes at a time.
During degraded operation, read access may continue if the data is still verified.
Questionable or partially updated state shall be held back until it is confirmed safe.
The system shall prevent unauthorized access, overwrite, and data-corruption scenarios.
A service shall not be able to write into another service's memory.
A service shall not be able to commit stale state after its lane has already been superseded.
A faulty component shall not be able to corrupt shared mission data solely because it is still physically connected.
The system shall block accidental cross-writes during failover.
The surviving lane shall not inherit bad data from the failed side during failover.
Degraded reads shall be allowed when the system can confirm that the data comes from a healthy lane or from a previously validated state that has not been contradicted by current fault detection.
The system shall expose data that is only slightly delayed if it is still within the accepted freshness window and matches redundant cross-checks.
The system shall keep data hidden until it is verified or replaced if the value is partial, inconsistent between lanes, or outside the allowed age or confidence threshold.
Operators and oversight users may review degraded data only if the data is clearly labeled as degraded and they are not using it to drive an automatic control function.
If the system is in a validation gap, the system shall block operational use and allow read-only review at most.
During mission-critical changes or active fault recovery, access shall be limited to the smallest set of authorized personnel.
During mission-critical changes or active fault recovery, access shall be kept read-only unless there is a specific approved action needed to restore safety.
The stakeholder list shall be recorded as undecided for now.
Specific user groups shall not be named until the operational roles and the personnel assigned to the flight software support chain are confirmed.

The system shall allow a controlled recovery path only if the fault-tolerant layer has isolated the bad component, validated the surviving data against a trusted copy or quorum, and explicitly re-authorized the transfer.
The smallest authorized read-only group shall be able to inspect status.
The smallest authorized read-only group shall be able to confirm which lane is healthy.
The smallest authorized read-only group shall be able to review fault logs.
The smallest authorized read-only group shall be able to verify whether a switchover or rollback has already happened.
If there is an approved recovery procedure, the smallest authorized read-only group shall be able to request it or authorize the next step.
The smallest authorized read-only group shall not directly alter mission data unless that authority is explicitly granted for the event.
Access shall stay blocked entirely if identity cannot be verified.
Access shall stay blocked entirely if the system cannot confirm the current lane state.
Access shall stay blocked entirely if a recovery action would risk propagating stale or corrupted data.
During takeover, the system shall remap task state only through a defined, prevalidated state model.
During takeover, the system shall not copy raw memory from the failed lane when remapping task state.
Any task state resumed on the healthy lane shall be checked for completeness, version compatibility, and freshness.
If a task state cannot be translated safely, the system shall restart it from a known safe checkpoint instead of guessing the state.
The fault-tolerant service shall preserve mission-approved configuration that is common to both lanes during a switchover.
The fault-tolerant service shall preserve timing parameters during a switchover.
The fault-tolerant service shall preserve service policy during a switchover.
The fault-tolerant service shall preserve validated task settings that are known to be current during a switchover.
The fault-tolerant service shall reset or recompute any value tied to a specific lane on the healthy side during a switchover.
The fault-tolerant service shall reset or recompute transient fault state on the healthy side during a switchover.
The fault-tolerant service shall reset or recompute cached status on the healthy side during a switchover.
The fault-tolerant service shall reset or recompute values that may have been learned after the last safe checkpoint on the healthy side during a switchover.
The fault-tolerant service shall exclude any value that cannot be proven current and portable from the switchover.
A replacement service that is purely observational or can run without affecting control decisions may be introduced gradually alongside the old service for comparison and validation.

A replacement service that participates in scheduling must not replace the old service until it has been proven equivalent under representative fault conditions and across the same timing and recovery scenarios.

A replacement service that participates in failover must not replace the old service until it has been proven equivalent under representative fault conditions and across the same timing and recovery scenarios.

A replacement service that participates in any mission-critical decision path must not replace the old service until it has been proven equivalent under representative fault conditions and across the same timing and recovery scenarios.
A parallel rollout is allowed only when the new service can be kept isolated from the authoritative path and can be rolled back immediately if its results diverge.
A replacement service may run in parallel as a shadow instance only if it is fully isolated from mission authority.
A shadow instance must receive the same inputs as the active service.
A shadow instance's outputs must be compared only against the trusted lane and must not affect flight behavior.
A shadow instance may be used while the system is still confirming timing equivalence.
A shadow instance may be used while the system is still confirming state-handling equivalence.
A shadow instance may be used while the system is still confirming fault-recovery equivalence.
The shadow-instance role is especially acceptable after a software change or a hardware swap.
The shadow instance must be removed from that role immediately if any output mismatch exceeds tolerance.
The shadow instance must be removed from that role immediately if it misses timing deadlines.
The shadow instance must be removed from that role immediately if corrupted input is detected.
The shadow instance must be removed from that role immediately if it shows unexpected resource growth.
The shadow instance must be removed from that role immediately if it influences shared state or masks a lane fault.
The system shall allow a limited mismatch or delay to be tolerated briefly when it is known to be tied to a specific transient fault.
The system shall allow tolerance only when the shadow instance remains within a predefined safe envelope.
The system shall keep the shadow instance in the comparison role only if the deviation is shrinking and is not affecting any authoritative path.
The system shall remove the shadow instance immediately if the mismatch grows, persists past the allowed window, or appears ambiguous.
The system shall allow bypassing or deferring an interaction only under tightly controlled recovery rules.
The system shall allow switching to an approved alternate interface only when the normal path is compromised.
Any bypass, deferral, or alternate-interface choice shall be predefined and logged.
The system shall not allow a bypass, deferral, or alternate-interface choice that violates safety constraints or corrupts shared state.
The system shall function as the fault-tolerant computing layer for the X-38’s redundant flight-critical computer.
The system shall sit underneath the mission applications and provide them with reliable timing services.
The vehicle shall keep operating safely even if parts of the computing system fail.
The software shall detect faults.
The software shall coordinate the redundant resources without requiring the applications to manage that complexity themselves.
The system shall provide predictable scheduling.
The primary users of the X-38 Fault Tolerant System Services are the mission applications and the flight software that run on top of the service layer.
The X-38 flight software engineers are real decision-makers for the X-38 Fault Tolerant System Services.
Systems engineers are real decision-makers for the X-38 Fault Tolerant System Services.
Mission operations personnel are real decision-makers for the X-38 Fault Tolerant System Services.
Safety and verification teams are involved with the X-38 Fault Tolerant System Services because they care about how faults are isolated and what happens during reconfiguration or recovery.
Integration and test teams are heavily involved with the X-38 Fault Tolerant System Services because they need to validate the behavior under failure scenarios before flight.
Stakeholders shall work from the same set of interface and behavior definitions.
Stakeholders shall agree on what a fault looks like.
Flight software engineers shall own the implementation details.
Safety and operations stakeholders shall define the acceptable failure modes.
Disagreements shall be settled through the systems engineering process and formal review boards.
The system shall maintain consistency in a flight-critical system.
The organization shall maintain a controlled glossary.
The systems team shall define the canonical meaning of terms such as fault, failure, isolation, reconfiguration, and redundancy.
Ambiguous terms shall be clarified during review instead of being left open.
The teams shall integrate the fault-tolerant services with the flight applications.
The teams shall verify that the scheduling paths behave correctly.
The teams shall verify that the communication paths behave correctly.
The teams shall exercise failure cases in test.
The system shall recover as expected after a processor, task, or data path is lost.
The teams shall tighten the interfaces.
The teams shall clean up any issues found during integration.
The system shall be stable before it can support mission use.
The system shall handle faults that can disable one side of the redundant computing path.
Operational faults may present as missed deadlines.
Operational faults may present as bad data.
Operational faults may present as a module failing to respond.
The system shall isolate the bad element when a fault is detected.
The system shall shift work to surviving resources when a fault is detected.
The system shall handle transient faults that clear up on their own.
The fault-tolerant system shall be especially critical during dynamic flight phases in which the vehicle relies on tight control loops and has very little margin for interruption.
The system shall provide seamless redundancy and recovery when it is reconfiguring after a fault.
The system shall provide seamless redundancy and recovery while carrying out a safety-critical command sequence.
A brief disruption during these critical phases is unacceptable.
Mission operations personnel shall interact with the fault-tolerant system through higher-level command and monitoring paths rather than directly through the fault-tolerant services.
Hardware subsystems shall communicate through defined interfaces for data exchange and command control.
The service layer shall ensure that the rest of the vehicle sees a consistent view of what is still healthy.
The system shall keep terminology in the official requirements and interface documents.
The system shall manage health and status records for processors, tasks, memory regions, and communication channels.
The system shall track timing information, fault indications, and the current redundancy state.
The system shall preserve command and telemetry data consistently during reconfiguration so the vehicle does not lose control context.
The system shall treat an out-of-bounds condition as a fault indication.
The system shall consult the redundancy state to determine what can safely take over.
The system shall copy or reestablish the needed context if possible.
During a fault, the system must ensure that any in-flight command or control state is safely completed, rolled back, or transferred to the surviving side.
The system must prevent the vehicle from being left in an ambiguous condition during a fault.
The system must keep telemetry and status data consistent enough for flight software and mission operations to trust the vehicle state.
If a piece of state cannot be preserved safely, the system should fail in a controlled way.
The system must not continue using stale or partial data when a piece of state cannot be preserved safely.
The system shall continuously collect data from the computer and subsystem monitors.
The fault-tolerant services shall process collected data in near real time.
Some data shall be retained only long enough to support immediate decisions and failover.
Selected status and event records shall be retained for post-flight analysis and engineering review.
The data shall be available with very low latency.
The data shall be protected from corruption.
The data shall be handled in a way that continues to work under radiation, memory faults, and limited onboard resources.
The system shall use redundancy wherever practical.
The system shall apply redundancy especially for the most critical state and the services that manage it.
The system shall ensure that a single failure does not take out the vehicle’s control path.
The system’s protections shall be lightweight enough to meet real-time flight deadlines.
The system’s protections shall be deterministic enough to meet real-time flight deadlines.
The system shall not use safeguards that add too much latency.
The system shall run on the flight-qualified hardware that is provided.
The system shall operate within tight memory limits.
The system shall operate within tight processor margin limits.
The system shall operate within tight timing limits.
The software shall not assume extra capacity.
The software shall not assume dynamic behavior that would be acceptable on a ground system.
The system shall comply with NASA flight software assurance and verification expectations.
The system design shall be traceable.
The system design shall be testable.
The system design shall be predictable enough to support certification reviews.
The system architecture shall be built around redundant lanes.
The system architecture shall include explicit fault isolation.
The system must comply with NASA and project-level assurance standards.
The system must follow the normal safety and software verification practices used for crewed flight systems.
The system must maintain strong requirements traceability.
The system must have rigorous test evidence.
The system should include fault-injection or failure-mode coverage where possible.
The system must carefully document assumptions and recovery behavior.
The system design shall be driven by the need to prove what happens in every failure case.
The system shall keep interfaces explicit rather than implicit.
The system shall control state transitions rather than leaving them implicit.
The verification process shall include test cases for fault detection.
The verification process shall produce evidence that timing still holds under fault detection, lane takeover, degraded operation, and recovery conditions.
Reviews shall be formal and multi-step.
Flight software engineers shall interact with the fault-tolerant system through status displays.
Flight software engineers shall interact with the fault-tolerant system through logs.
Flight software engineers shall interact with the fault-tolerant system through commanded test or configuration interfaces.
Mission operations personnel shall use system information to monitor health and react to off-nominal events.
Fault reports shall be precise enough to be actionable.
Fault reports shall avoid overwhelming users with low-level diagnostics.
The system shall present the detected fault.
The system shall present the current redundancy state.
The system shall present the recovery action that the system has taken or is about to take.
The system shall support human monitoring and confirmation rather than requiring improvisation under time pressure during a fault.
The system shall provide telemetry summaries, fault logs, and health/status pages for engineers and mission operations personnel during fault analysis.
If a manual action is needed, the tools shall make the current state and the allowed recovery options very obvious.
The system shall prioritize the fault summary first.
When the system is under stress, it shall report the same fault condition in the same terms and with the same cues.
The interface shall allow the operator to drill into details only when needed.
The system shall support training for new users.
The system shall provide structured reference material.
The system shall provide scenario-based walkthroughs for common faults.
The system shall show what the system does automatically during fault scenarios.
The system shall show what a human is expected to verify during fault scenarios.
The system shall provide concise help text.
The system shall include fault examples in logs or training mode.
The system shall avoid exposing unnecessary internal details in routine outputs.
The handling rules for any data that leaves the vehicle or is stored for post-flight analysis shall be confirmed.
The system shall maintain separation between operational channels and any downlinked or stored records.
During recovery, security measures shall not interfere with the fault response.
Protection mechanisms shall be lightweight and fail safely.
Data leaving the vehicle shall typically be limited to approved telemetry and fault artifacts.
The system shall treat internal communications as operational data rather than open-text records.
The system shall maintain strong separation between flight-critical services and services used for analysis or ground interaction.
Fault recovery paths shall remain available even if a security service is degraded.
Security protections shall not become a single point of failure.
Access on board should be enforced more by partitioning and fixed interfaces than by a heavy interactive login model.
Authorized users and systems should be identified by their role and by which bus or service endpoint they are allowed to communicate with.
The system is expected to use a combination of trusted partitions, service-level permissions, and authenticated links for anything that crosses subsystem boundaries.
The flight computer is expected not to use a user-style login.
Safety and continued vehicle operation shall have the highest priority.
Fault detection and isolation shall be treated as must-have requirements, even if they consume some resources.
Availability shall be the next priority after safety and continued vehicle operation.
The system should keep mission-critical functions running.
Some extra overhead or degraded performance is acceptable if needed to preserve control and redundancy.
Requirement priorities shall be agreed among the flight software, avionics, and mission assurance teams.
Requirement priorities shall be documented in the system requirements baseline and reviewed in formal design and safety reviews.
The system shall check protections at service boundaries rather than inside every recovery action.
The system shall keep fault logic fast and predictable.
The system shall verify who or what is allowed to publish before a transaction is accepted.
The system shall verify who or what is allowed to subscribe before a transaction is accepted.
The system shall verify who or what is allowed to retrieve data before a transaction is accepted.
The recovery path shall run with minimal extra steps once a fault is detected.
If a security function fails, the system shall degrade in a controlled way rather than block fault detection or isolation.
The system shall usually normalize data as it moves between onboard services and post-flight analysis tools.
The system shall perform normalization when different components store or publish data in different internal formats.
The system shall preserve a canonical meaning for each data item.
The system shall retain fixed metadata timestamps for each data item.
The system shall retain fixed metadata source identifiers for each data item.
The system shall retain fixed metadata sequence information for each data item.
Fault state must not be converted like ordinary telemetry because it is time-sensitive and tied to the exact redundancy configuration at the moment an event occurs.
The on-board representation should remain stable for as long as possible.
When an update is unavoidable, the system shall provide explicit versioning and translation rules so old and new formats can coexist during the transition.
The update process shall preserve enough history and active fault context to allow safe recovery if a reset or switchover occurs during migration.
Any version transition must prove itself before it is trusted in flight.
The system shall provide a conservative fallback path that reverts to the last known good version or state if the new version or state does not reconcile cleanly.
If a mismatch appears during migration, the system shall isolate the update path and keep the existing fault management logic running rather than allowing the inconsistency to spread.
The system shall convert data through well-defined service interfaces.
The system shall protect data integrity by performing validation checks when data is packaged, transferred, and unpacked.
The system shall export onboard records in a form that can be traced back to the original event without losing sequence or correlation information.
The system shall give fault management higher operational priority than nonessential security checks once a critical event is underway.
The system shall enforce access control and data protection on normal service entry points.
The system shall preserve the fault response first and defer less critical actions until the vehicle is stable again when there is a conflict.
The system shall use strong separation between the safety-critical fault management components and the general mission software.
Trusted components shall handle the minimum necessary coordination for fault detection, voting, and recovery.
Less trusted applications shall communicate only through controlled interfaces and limited message paths.
The system should handle cases where a security service is slow during a recovery action.
During a transition, the system shall keep one fault data format authoritative while introducing the new format in parallel.

If the new fault data format disagrees with the older trusted state, the system shall keep the older trusted state active until the new format proves it has the same fault context and redundancy picture.
